An in-place runtime upgrade can address a modernization problem without moving data ownership only when the driver is lifecycle or security support - a documented unsupported runtime or dependency - and the existing public API and persisted state need not move. Declared costs: runtime/library compatibility, old data encoding and mixed-version release.

By default it keeps the externally visible state owner unchanged, using branch-by-abstraction or a compatible migration step where internal changes cannot be made atomically, rather than reassigning data ownership. The upgrade is proven in stages: the old version unaffected under additive interfaces/schema (T1); cross-version reads/writes, idempotency and rejection in the mixed T2 phase; promotion only after measured SLO and data-integrity gates (T3); cleanup only when no historic replay requires the old encoding (T4).

The alternative is falsified when the required dependency/runtime combination cannot run or externally required behavior cannot be preserved. A new database alone does not make a replacement authoritative while two writers accept edits without a conflict-resolution rule; dual write without a coordinated correctness protocol is not atomic commit.

A precondition is that the modernization outcome is defined independently of technology, for example removing a documented unsupported dependency without invalidating persisted data or external contracts, because age alone does not explain failure and an unknown issue requires investigation, not a design imperative.
